title: Verifier-Backed Hard Problem Generation for Mathematical Reasoning
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: A verifier gates generated problems for validity, while solver outcomes feed back difficulty, so the generator learns to produce valid, hard items.
layout: Single panel, cyclic loop of five nodes, dashed feedback arrows on top and left
description: A single-panel cyclic diagram with five rounded boxes in a loop. The top row runs left to right: a blue Setter Q (robot icon), dashed Candidate pairs (x, y*) with a question-mark document, and a green Verifier V (shield with checkmark). Arrows are labeled 'generate' and 'check correctness'. A 'pass' arrow runs down to a green dashed box, Verified pairs (x, y*), which has a check icon. A 'train' arrow runs left to the orange Solver S (robot icon). From the Solver, dashed orange arrows lead to a box of sampled attempts, 'Try 1 ✓, Try 2 ✗, … Try n ✓', labeled 'sample S(x) multiple times'. A dashed teal 'validity feedback (pass/fail)' arrow runs from the Verifier back to the Setter across the top. A dashed orange 'difficulty feedback' arrow runs up from the attempts box to the Setter. Color codes the roles: blue for setter, green for verifier, orange for solver. The eye goes first to the Setter and the robot icons.
caption: VHG framework. The setter proposes problem-reference pairs, the verifier gates validity, and accepted pairs are scored by solver difficulty for training and challenge construction.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capability in solving scientific and mathematical problems, yet they struggle to produce valid and challenging novel problems -- an essential component for advancing LLM training and enabling autonomous scientific research. Existing problem generation approaches either depend on expensive human expert involvement or adopt naive self-play paradigms, which frequently yield invalid problems due to reward hacking. This work introduces VHG, a verifier-backed hard problem generation framework built upon three-party self-play. By integrating an independent verifier into the conventional setter-solver duality, our design constrains the setter's reward to be jointly determined by problem validity (evaluated by the verifier) and difficulty (assessed by the solver). We instantiate two verifier variants: a Hard symbolic verifier and a Soft LLM-based verifier, with evaluations conducted on indefinite integral tasks and general mathematical reasoning tasks. Experimental results show that VHG substantially outperforms all baseline methods by a clear margin. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/VHG.
